content.text:
Let me untangle two things first: `senderRef` is a **different fix** (fix 3, the profile-name one — yes, it just copies `msg.contact.name` onto the sender when Meta includes it). The reply fix is `withReplyContext`. Let me trace it end-to-end with real data so you can see exactly what happens and why the stub exists.

**Step 1 — what arrives.** Customer long-presses your message "your order shipped!", taps Reply, types "when exactly?". Meta's webhook (via the SDK) delivers:

```js
{
  id: "wamid.NEW123",
  from: "919820529309",
  content: { type: "text", body: "when exactly?" },
  context: { id: "wamid.SHIPPED456", from: "15550001111" }  // ← the quote marker
}
```

That `context` field is the *entire* signal that this was a reply. Before the fix, nothing read it — `mapContent` returned `asText("when exactly?")` and the quote relationship evaporated. That's literally Pratik's screenshot.

**Step 2 — what `withReplyContext` does with it.** After `mapContent` produces the inner content, `toMessages` passes it through `withReplyContext(msg, content)`, which asks two questions:

1. Is `msg.context?.id` present? No → return content unchanged (the common case, zero behavior change).
2. Is the event type in `REPLY_EXEMPT_TYPES`? Yes → return unchanged, because for those events `context.id` means something else (a button tap's context points at the button message — that's plumbing, not a human quoting).

Otherwise it wraps:

```js
{
  type: "reply",
  content: { type: "text", text: "when exactly?" },
  target: { id: "wamid.SHIPPED456", content: { type: "custom", raw: { whatsapp_type: "reply-target", stub: true } } }
}
```

**Step 3 — why the target is a stub.** A `reply`'s target is supposed to be the *quoted message*. But look at what Meta gave us in step 1: just the wamid. Not the text, not the type, nothing — and critically, **the Cloud API has no "fetch message by id" endpoint**, so we can't go get it either. (iMessage can — its server has `messages.get` — which is why iMessage replies are richer.) So the target is the honest maximum: a real `id` (the wamid your app already has, since it received or sent that message earlier) plus a placeholder content marked `stub: true` so nobody mistakes it for the actual quoted text. Same trade-off the codebase already made for reactions (`reaction-target` stub) — a reaction event also only tells you *which* message was reacted to, not what it said.

The app's job then: `message.content.target.id` → look up `wamid.SHIPPED456` in its own message history (it saw that message go by) → knows the customer is asking about the shipping notice. The *relationship* is what was lost and is now restored; the content lookup was always going to be the app's.

**Step 4 — how we know it works.** Three levels:

- The tests don't unit-test `withReplyContext` in isolation — they drive the **real production path**: `messages([fakeClient])` → `clientStream` → the actual `toMessages`/`mapContent` code, with a fake client whose event stream yields the exact payload shapes from step 1. Then they assert on the shape that comes out the other end — the same shape the platform layer ships to your app. Seven scenarios: plain quote, no context, quoted captioned media (reply wrapping a group), quoted contact card, button tap NOT wrapped, reaction NOT wrapped, and the poison-event one (a context-carrying event that crashes mapping gets skipped, stream survives, next message still flows reply-wrapped).
- Upstream data shape: Meta's webhook docs confirm `context: { from, id }` on quoted replies, and the SDK's mapping code (`mapInboundMessage`) confirms it's passed through — so the fake payloads in the tests match reality.
- The one thing the tests *can't* prove is a live Meta round-trip. If you want that, the real verification is exactly Pratik's repro: quote-reply a business message on a test number and watch the webhook — it should now read `type: "reply"` with a `target.id`, matching the iMessage payload shape from his screenshot.

One honest limitation to be upfront about (it's in the PR description): iMessage's webhook shows a `contentPreview` of the quoted text; ours can't, because we never have the quoted content — only its id. Fixing that would need the cache-enrichment option you deferred (remember recently-seen messages by wamid, attach their content when quoted). The id is delivered today; the preview is the future nice-to-have.

content.text:
Right. Meta's Cloud API is strictly forward-only: webhooks push events at you once, and there's no `GET /message/{wamid}` — no history endpoint, no search, nothing. If you didn't record a message when it flew past, it's gone from your view forever (Meta explicitly expects businesses to store their own message history; they even stop redelivering webhook events after a short retry window). That's a deliberate design stance of theirs, not an SDK gap — which is why the audit classified anything needing lookback as "platform limitation."

iMessage is the opposite world: the Mac's `chat.db` holds the full history, so the server can `messages.get(guid)` anytime — that's why its reply targets arrive with real content and a `contentPreview`, and ours arrive with an id and a stub.

The only workaround is the one you deferred: since every message *does* flow through the provider once (inbound via the stream, outbound via send), keep a small LRU of recently-seen messages keyed by wamid, and when a quote references one still in cache, attach its real content to the target. That gets you `contentPreview` parity for recent quotes — but it's best-effort by nature (restart, eviction, or a multi-process deploy and the cache misses, falling back to the stub anyway — same known weakness as the existing poll/reaction caches). A *durable* version would need Photon's gateway to store history server-side, which is a `whatsapp-server`/SDK change, not a spectrum-ts one.

For the apps that matter here, the id alone is usually enough — they're already persisting their own conversation history, so `target.id` is a key into data they have.

content.text:
Next up: **fix 2, inbound voice notes** (`dcf6e49`) — the smallest one, so this'll be quick.

**The problem.** WhatsApp has two kinds of audio: a forwarded MP3 file, and a push-to-talk voice note recorded with the mic button. On the phone they look completely different (file card vs. waveform bubble), and apps care about the difference — a voice-agent product wants to transcribe voice notes, not cover songs. Meta tells them apart with one field:

```js
content: {
  type: "audio",
  media: { id: "9836...", mimeType: "audio/ogg; codecs=opus", voice: true }  // ← PTT marker
}
```

Before the fix, `mapContent`'s media case shoved *everything* — image, video, document, audio, voice notes — through `lazyMedia`, which always builds `asAttachment`. The `voice` flag was never read, so a voice note arrived at your app as a generic file attachment. (iMessage got the equivalent fix in #199, which is what made this a parity gap.)

**The change.** Two parts:

1. The old `lazyMedia` body got split: `lazyMediaSource` builds the shared lazy-download plumbing (`id`, `name`, `mimeType`, and `read()`/`stream()` closures that fetch bytes from the media endpoint on demand), and then `lazyMedia` = `asAttachment(source)`, `lazyVoice` = `asVoice(source)`. Pure refactor — the download logic is written once, only the Spectrum wrapper differs.
2. One branch in the media case: `content.type === "audio" && content.media.voice` → `lazyVoice`, else `lazyMedia` as before.

**What to scrutinize:** that the branch is `&&` on both conditions — an image or document can never take the voice path, and audio *without* the flag (`voice` absent or false) still becomes an attachment, byte-for-byte the old behavior. The blast radius is exactly "audio events where Meta set `voice: true`," which previously didn't exist as a distinguishable category at all.

**How we know it works:** `test/inbound-voice.test.ts` drives the real stream path with both payloads — `voice: true` + the real-world mime (`audio/ogg; codecs=opus`) asserts `type: "voice"` comes out, and plain `audio/mpeg` without the flag asserts `type: "attachment"` (the no-regression case). Core-side safety was verified during planning: `voice` is a long-standing content type in the union (iMessage emits it), and the webhook serializer round-trips it, so nothing downstream chokes on the new shape. And Meta's docs confirm the field: *"voice: boolean indicating if audio is a recording made with the WhatsApp client voice recording feature."*

**Fix 3 (sender name, `448304e`)** — you actually already read this one correctly earlier: `senderRef` takes `msg.contact?.name` (the customer's WhatsApp profile "push name," which Meta sends in `contacts[].profile.name` alongside most inbound messages) and spreads it onto `sender` as `{ id, name }`. The two things worth a glance:

- `src/types.ts`: `userSchema` grew the optional `name` field — that's the schema that types `message.sender` for this platform.
- The guard matters: Meta doesn't *guarantee* the contacts payload, so when it's absent `sender` must be exactly `{ id }` — not `{ id, name: undefined }`, which is why it's a conditional spread rather than a plain assignment. The test asserts with `toEqual` (strict shape match) on both cases, plus that the name propagates onto each item of a captioned-media group (those group items carry their own sender copies because cloud webhook delivery serializes them per-item).

Both are pure inbound additions — neither touches the send path or adds a throw that isn't inside the stream's poison guard. When you've eyeballed those, the remaining two are the link previews (four call sites, all the same one-liner) and the partial-send error policy — say the word and I'll walk those.

content.text:
Full audit done. Verdict: **everything checks out except one real gap — and it's exactly the thing you asked about.** `sender.name` does not survive webhook delivery.

Here's the complete trace, layer by layer:

**✅ What's proper:**
- **`reply` and `voice` content** — both are registered arms in spectrum-webhook's serializer (`KNOWN_CONTENT_TYPES`, dedicated `serializeReply`/`serializeVoice`), so the new inbound shapes ship as proper typed wire content, not unknown blobs.
- **The reply-target stub is safe** — this was my main worry mid-trace. spectrum-webhook's `serializeMessageRef` calls `target.timestamp.toISOString()` unguarded and our stub has no timestamp, *but* core's `wrapProviderMessage` inflates nested reply/reaction targets before delivery ever sees them: `timestamp: raw.timestamp ?? new Date()` (`build.ts:516`) and platform stamping via `buildMessage`. Reaction stubs — identical shape — have shipped through this exact path all along; replies ride the same rails (`build.ts:560-566`). No crash, no stream risk.
- **Group items** — `serializeGroup` recurses full `serializeMessage` per item, which is precisely why `groupItem` carries sender/space/timestamp (that crash was already fixed in a past PR; our items comply).
- **Reply on the wire** looks like: `target: { id, platform, timestamp, sender }` — no `contentPreview` since that's only populated for text targets and ours is the custom stub. Known, documented limitation.

**❌ The gap — `sender.name`:**

```
provider:  sender: { id, name: "Pratik Jain" }        ✓ (fix 3)
core:      { ...sender, __platform }  → name survives  ✓ (build.ts spreads it, "inbound senders passed through untouched")
in-process apps:  message.sender.name                  ✓ works today
spectrum-webhook: serializeUser = { id, platform }     ✗ name DROPPED here
webhook consumers:                                      ✗ never see it
```

`serializeUser` (`spectrum-webhook/src/delivery/serialize.ts:359`) hand-projects exactly two fields. So fix 3 is real for anyone running Spectrum in-process, but webhook consumers — which is how Pratik's team integrates — won't get the name until spectrum-webhook forwards it.

**The fix is small and backward-safe:** add `name` to `SerializedUser` + conditionally spread it in `serializeUser` (one-line change in the spectrum-webhook repo), and optionally add `readonly name?: string` to core's `User` interface in spectrum-ts so it's typed rather than runtime-only. The receiving SDK already tolerates it — `slimSenderSchema` is a `looseObject` and the deserializer spreads the whole sender, so older SDK versions won't break when the field appears.

That's a PR in a different repo (`photon-hq/spectrum-webhook`, your checkout is at `~/Developer/photon-ai/spectrum-webhook`). Want me to make it — the `serializeUser` change plus a test there, and the optional `User.name?` typing addition to #201?
